analysis.subject: earth-science
analysis.pageCoverage: Page explains how thermal characteristics, composition, movement and density define atmospheric layers, describes each layer from the outer exosphere to the lower troposphere, and details temperature trends and transition boundaries.

overview.headline: Vertical structure of the atmosphere and how temperature varies with height

keyPoints.point: Students learn that the envelope of gas surrounding Earth changes from the ground up through layered structure.
keyPoints.quote: The envelope of gas surrounding the Earth changes from the ground up.

keyPoints.point: Students learn that absorption in the thermosphere causes temperature to increase with height.
keyPoints.quote: Because of this absorption, the temperature increases with height.

keyPoints.point: Students learn that temperature increases with height in the stratosphere due to ozone formation.
keyPoints.quote: In this region, the temperature increases with height.

keyPoints.point: Students learn that as density of gases decrease with height the air becomes thinner in the troposphere.
keyPoints.quote: As the density of the gases in this layer decrease with height, the air becomes thinner.

keyPoints.point: Students learn that gases in the mesosphere are thick enough to slow meteors which burn up as fiery trails.
keyPoints.quote: The gases in the mesosphere are now thick enough to slow down meteors hurtling into the atmosphere, where they burn up, leaving fiery trails in the night sky.

keyTerms.gloss: lowest layer where weather occurs and height varies with latitude
keyTerms.quote: The troposphere begins at the Earth's surface, but the height of the troposphere varies.

keyTerms.gloss: middle layer that extends above the surface and holds ozone that warms the air
keyTerms.quote: The stratosphere extends from 4 -12 miles (6-20 km) above the Earth's surface to around 31 miles (50 km).

keyTerms.gloss: middle layer where meteors slow and burn leaving fiery trails
keyTerms.quote: The gases in the mesosphere are now thick enough to slow down meteors hurtling into the atmosphere, where they burn up, leaving fiery trails in the night sky.

keyTerms.gloss: upper atmosphere layer known for rising temperature due to solar radiation absorption
keyTerms.quote: Between about 53 miles (85 km) and 375 miles (600 km) lies the thermosphere, known as the upper atmosphere.

keyTerms.gloss: transition boundary that marks the bottom of the stratosphere
keyTerms.quote: The transition layer at the bottom of the stratosphere is called the tropopause.

componentPlan.pedagogicalReason: helps students visualize the vertical stacking of layers in page order and link each boundary to temperature changes
componentPlan.focusQuote: The five basic layers of the atmosphere

componentPlan.pedagogicalReason: reinforces factual recall of temperature trends and boundary names that define each layer
componentPlan.focusQuote: Each of the layers are bounded by "pauses" where the greatest changes in thermal characteristics, chemical composition, movement, and density occur.
